So the Blót for Frey was the other day. It's been so nice outside here since around then; I've been spending a lot more time outside doing chores and stuff than I'd usually be able to do around this time of year (when it's usually in the triple digits). Being able to connect with nature is rare for me around this time of year, and it's been really nice.

Some folks know this time of years as "Lammas." The name Lammas is taken from an Anglo-Saxon heathen festival which was forcibly Christianized. As the name (from hlaf-mass, "loaves festival") implies, it is a feast of thanksgiving for bread, symbolizing the first fruits of the harvest. Heathens mark the holiday by baking a figure of the God Freyr in bread, and then symbolically sacrificing and eating it. In English and German tradition, the First Sheaf was often bound and blessed as an offering to Heathen deities, or the spirits of the field at the beginning of harvest - just as the Last Sheaf was at its end. English folk custom also includes the decoration of wells and springs at this time.

To my (and generally on this site, OUR) ancestors, the feast was especially thought of as holy to Freyr, as a fertility God, Thor, as a harvest God, and to his wife Sif, whose long golden hair can be seen in the rippling fields of ripe grain.

The warriors who had gone off to fight at the end of planting season have come back around this time, loaded with a summer's worth of plunder, and ready to reap the crops that had ripened while they'd been gone a'viking.

"Loaf-Feast" (Lammas) is the end of the summer's vacation and the beginning of a time of hard work which lasts through the next two or three months, while we ready ourselves for the winter.
